labelChirho: Hifil: to strike in battle, smite enemies
descriptionChirho: The primary military Hifil sense of נכה: to strike, smite, or attack an enemy in warfare, encompassing striking persons, armies, and cities in battle narratives; all languages uniformly use generic 'strike' vocabulary (Arabic ضَرَبَ, Swahili -piga, Korean 치다, Spanish golpear/herir) without specialized martial terms, indicating the base combative sense.

labelChirho: Hifil: to strike with affliction, plague
descriptionChirho: A specialized Hifil sense where God or a divine agent strikes with plague, disease, blindness, or curse as punishment; distinguished by English 'with blindness' (117685), patterns of divine first-person declarations ('I will strike you'), and lament addresses to God ('have You struck us'), reflecting the Deuteronomic curse formula and prophetic judgment oracles.

The Hifil sense of נכה for non-lethal, non-military physical striking: beating, hitting, or disciplining a person; distinguished by Korean 때리다 (beat, hit personally) instead of generic 치다, Spanish 'azotes' (lashes/stripes) for punishment, imperative commands to strike in personal rather than battle contexts, and participial legal formulas describing 'the one who strikes' in casuistic law.

The Hifil sense of נכה where the direct object is a non-personal entity such as a land, city, body of water, rock, or ground; identified by feminine pronominal suffixes (הָ/אֹתָהּ) and neuter 'it' in English glosses, with Swahili forms using object-class prefixes (i-/li-) rather than personal prefixes (m-/wa-).

A specialized Hifil sense of נכה where the striking causes wounding or injury without death; distinguished by Arabic جَرَحَ (جرح, to wound) instead of the usual ضَرَبَ, and English 'wounded' rather than 'struck', indicating the translators perceived bodily injury as the focus rather than the blow itself.

labelChirho: Hifil: to strike dead, kill, slay
descriptionChirho: A lethal sense of the Hifil where the striking results in death; distinguished by glosses such as Spanish 'mataron/matador' (they killed / killer), Arabic 'يَقْتُل' (to kill), and Swahili 'kuwaua/kumuua' (to kill), indicating the action goes beyond mere hitting to a fatal blow or killing.

A figurative or military sense of the Hifil meaning to defeat, overcome, or conquer an opponent; distinguished by glosses such as Spanish 'vencer/venciere/derrotar' (conquer/overcome/defeat) and Swahili 'kushinda' (to defeat/overcome), indicating triumph over an adversary rather than mere physical striking.

A specialized Hifil sense denoting thrusting or stabbing with a pointed instrument rather than a blow; distinguished by Spanish 'metia' (thrust in), Korean '찔렀다' (pierced/stabbed), and Swahili 'akachoma' (he stabbed/pierced).

A metaphorical extension of the Hifil 'strike' applied to clapping or striking the hands together; distinguished by glosses such as English 'clapped', Spanish 'batieron' (they clapped), and Arabic 'safaquu' (they clapped).

A specialized Hifil sense denoting driving in or hammering a peg, stake, or nail; distinguished by Spanish 'echara' (will cast/drive) and Korean '박으리라' (will drive/nail in), indicating forceful insertion rather than a blow to a person.

The Hofal (causative passive) of נכה, meaning to be struck, smitten, or beaten; used of persons or cities that have been hit, attacked, or afflicted, including participles describing the state of being wounded or slain.
The Niphal (simple passive) of נכה, meaning to be struck or smitten; a rare passive form indicating the subject receives the blow.

The Pual (intensive passive) of נכה, meaning to be struck, blighted, or ruined; used of things destroyed or devastated, with Hindi glosses 'nash ho gaye' (were destroyed) suggesting a more thorough affliction.
The Piel (intensive active) of נכה, meaning to strike repeatedly or intensively; a rare stem for this root indicating intensified or repeated striking action.
